claims.claim: Both bacterial and human Hsp70 chaperones interact with clients by selecting the unfolded state from a pre-existing array of interconverting structures.
claims.source: Our measurements establish that both bacterial and human Hsp70 chaperones interact with clients by selecting the unfolded state from a pre-existing array of interconverting structures, suggesting a conserved mode of client recognition among Hsp70s and highlighting the importance of molecular dynamics in this recognition event.
claims.evidence: This is the main finding of the study as stated in the abstract, supported by NMR measurements described throughout the manuscript.

claims.claim: The Hsp70 family of molecular chaperones occupies a central node in the chaperone network.
claims.source: The Hsp70 family of molecular chaperones occupies a central node in this network, steering proteins synthesized on the ribosome to their native conformations, as well as cooperating with the machinery of protein disaggregation, refolding and proteolysis to control the fate of improperly folded and aggregated cellular proteins (Mayer and Bukau, 2005; Mayer, 2013; Mogk et al., 2015; Rosenzweig et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: Hsp70 interacts with client substrates via an ATP-dependent chaperone cycle that is tightly regulated by Hsp40 co-chaperones and nucleotide exchange factors (NEFs).
claims.source: Hsp70 interacts with client substrates via an ATP-dependent chaperone cycle that is tightly regulated by Hsp40 co-chaperones and nucleotide exchange factors (NEFs) (Balchin et al., 2016; Mayer and Bukau, 2005; Mayer, 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: Hsp70 is a 70 kDa protein that consists of a 45 kDa N-terminal ATPase domain (NBD) and a 25 kDa C-terminal substrate binding domain (SBD).
claims.source: Hsp70 is a 70 kDa protein that consists of a 45 kDa N-terminal ATPase domain (NBD) and a 25 kDa C-terminal substrate binding domain (SBD) (Figure 1A) (Mayer and Bukau, 2005).
claims.evidence: This structural information is supported by citation and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: The substrate binds in an extended conformation in the Hsp70 substrate binding domain.
claims.source: Crystal (Zhu et al., 1996; Zahn et al., 2013) and NMR structures (Stevens et al., 2003) of peptide-bound SBDs establish that the substrate binds in an extended conformation, with a 4–5 amino acid core of the substrate forming backbone hydrogen bonds as well as hydrophobic contacts with chaperone residues Val 436, Ile 401 and Ile 438 that line the SBD binding pocket (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This structural claim is supported by multiple citations to crystal and NMR structures and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: Hsp70 prefers substrate sequences enriched in large aliphatic hydrophobic sidechains such as Ile, Leu and Val.
claims.source: The hydrophobic nature of the central binding pocket governs the preference of Hsp70 for substrate sequences enriched in large aliphatic hydrophobic sidechains such as Ile, Leu and Val (Rüdiger et al., 1997).
claims.evidence: This claim about substrate preference is supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Full length protein substrates are globally unfolded in the Hsp70-bound state.
claims.source: Studies on full length protein substrates have revealed that these are globally unfolded in the Hsp70-bound state (Palleros et al., 1994; Kurt et al., 2006; Chen et al., 2006; Kurt and Cavagnero, 2008; Sharma et al., 2010; Kellner et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2015; Sekhar et al., 2015) and lack long-range interactions (Sekhar et al., 2016), though they can form local residual native (Sekhar et al., 2015) and non-native secondary structure (Kurt and Cavagnero, 2008) in regions far from the Hsp70 binding site.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior studies.

claims.claim: Hsp70 recognizes commonly occurring sequences in typical proteins with a frequency of about 1 in 40 residues.
claims.source: The ability of Hsp70 to recognize commonly occurring sequences in typical proteins with a frequency of about 1 in 40 residues makes it a promiscuous interactor (Rosenzweig et al., 2017), generating a highly heterogeneous Hsp70-substrate ensemble that ensures the efficient search of conformational space for an optimal folding pathway (Lee et al., 2015; Rosenzweig et al., 2017; Sekhar et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: Only an unfolded stretch of polypeptide can fit into the Hsp70 binding groove if the helical lid is closed.
claims.source: The structural constraints of the Hsp70 binding pocket (Figure 1C) are such that only an unfolded stretch of polypeptide can fit into the binding groove if the helical lid is closed (Zhu et al., 1996), though more compact protein conformations can be accommodated if the lid is partially open (Schlecht et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This structural constraint is supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: R17* is a three-helix bundle protein domain.
claims.source: R17* is a three-helix bundle protein domain (Figure 3A) with kinetics and thermodynamics of folding that suggest that it may be an ideal candidate for distinguishing between different Hsp70 binding mechanisms using the NMR approaches described above (Scott et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This structural description is supported by citation and illustrated in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: R17* has a strong predicted Hsp70 binding site with sidechains 41IQGLL45.
claims.source: R17* has a strong predicted (Rüdiger et al., 1997) Hsp70 binding site and the sidechains (41IQGLL45) forming this binding site are >40% solvent-exposed on average (Figure 3B), potentially facilitating binding of Hsp70 to the native protein along an IF pathway.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a prediction method and illustrated in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: Upon addition of DnaK/ATP to R17*, a new peak appears in the Met region of the 13C-1H HMQC spectrum that can be assigned to the bound state of R17*.
claims.source: Upon addition of 500 μM U-2H DnaK/ATP a new peak appears in the Met region of the 13C-1H HMQC spectrum that can be unambiguously assigned to the bound state of R17* (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from NMR data shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: Multiple bound conformations of the R17*-DnaK complex exist, interconverting with each other and with free DnaK in slow exchange on the NMR chemical shift timescale.
claims.source: The presence of several Ile 401 and Ile 438 resonances at distinct chemical shifts in the bound state demonstrates the existence of multiple bound conformations of the R17*-DnaK complex, interconverting with each other and with free DnaK in slow exchange on the NMR chemical shift timescale.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation of multiple distinct resonances in NMR spectra.

claims.claim: R17* is globally unfolded in the DnaK-bound state.
claims.source: Taken together, our data shows that DnaK-bound R17* is globally unfolded and resembles the U conformation of R17* that exists in equilibrium with N in the absence of DnaK.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is based on analysis of peak intensities in NMR spectra comparing native and unfolded states.

claims.claim: A pair of cross-peaks connecting the unfolded state of Met 26 with the bound state can be observed in the zz-exchange dataset for R17*.
claims.source: Figure 4A shows a 2D plane from the zz-exchange dataset acquired with a mixing time of 300 ms. A pair of cross-peaks can be observed, labeled 1 and 2, connecting the unfolded state of Met 26 with the bound state and assigning the bound resonance to the methyl group of Met 26.
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from the zz-exchange NMR experiment shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: There are no cross-peaks between the native state and the bound state of R17* in the zz-exchange experiment.
claims.source: Notably, there are no cross-peaks between N and the bound state, unequivocally demonstrating that DnaK interacts predominantly with the unfolded state of R17*.
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from the zz-exchange NMR experiment.

claims.claim: The fractional populations of N, U and B (bound) states of R17* are 58 ± 2%, 33 ± 1% and 9 ± 2%, respectively.
claims.source: On the basis of the relative fractional populations of N and U (pN/pU), as estimated from the first plane of the pseudo-3D zz-exchange dataset with TMIX = 25 ms (1.8:1) along with pU/pB (=kBU/kUB) values from the time-dependent zz-exchange data (3.4:1) pN, pU and pB (bound fraction) are calculated to be 58 ± 2%, 33 ± 1% and 9 ± 2%, respectively.
claims.evidence: These populations were calculated from zz-exchange data.

claims.claim: The relative partitioning of flux along the CS and IF pathways for R17* binding to DnaK is Θ > 113.
claims.source: From kUB = 0.8 s−1 and kNB <0.004 s−1, as well as pN/pU = 1.8, Θ >113.
claims.evidence: This flux ratio was calculated from rate constants and populations obtained from NMR data.

claims.claim: The mechanism of R17* binding to DnaK is overwhelmingly biased in favour of conformational selection.
claims.source: Flux measurements thus confirm that the mechanism of R17* binding to DnaK is overwhelmingly biased in favour of CS (Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: This conclusion is based on flux calculations from NMR data.

claims.claim: DrkN SH3 is a slow-folding protein with kex,UN ~ 1 s−1 at 20°C.
claims.source: DrkN SH3 is a slow-folding protein with kex,UN ~ 1 s−1, 20°C, and is marginally stable, populating a significant fraction of U at equilibrium (pN/pU ~ 2, pH 6.0, 20°C) (Farrow et al., 1994; Tollinger et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: This kinetic information is supported by citations to prior studies.

claims.claim: The DnaK bound state of drkN SH3 is structurally similar to the unfolded state.
claims.source: Previous studies have established that the DnaK bound state of drkN SH3 is structurally similar to U (Lee et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claims.claim: At least four new peaks appear in the methyl spectrum of drkN SH3 upon addition of DnaK/ATP.
claims.source: The binding of SH3 to DnaK can be clearly visualized through the appearance of at least four new peaks, labeled 1–4 in Figure 5D.
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from NMR data shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: Peaks 1 and 2 in the drkN SH3-DnaK complex arise from Ile at the 0 position of the DnaK binding site.
claims.source: Notably, there are NOEs connecting the two Ile peaks 1 and 2 of drkN SH3 to Ile 438 of the chaperone, indicating that peaks 1 and 2 arise from Ile at the 0 position of the DnaK binding site.
claims.evidence: This assignment is based on NOE data from a 3D NOESY experiment.

claims.claim: The native state CEST profiles of both Ile 27 and Ile 53 of drkN SH3 show only one minor dip each at the resonance frequencies of the corresponding unfolded states.
claims.source: The native state CEST profiles of both Ile 27 and Ile 53 show only one minor dip each, at the resonances frequencies of the corresponding 1Hδ1 shifts in their respective unfolded states.
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from CEST data shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: The CEST traces from both Ile 27 and Ile 53 in the unfolded state of drkN SH3 show minor dips to both the native state and the bound state.
claims.source: However, the corresponding CEST traces from both residues in U show minor dips to N as well as to the bound state, unambiguously demonstrating that the major flux for the binding reaction involves a pathway whereby DnaK selects the unfolded state of drkN SH3.
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from CEST data shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: The major flux for the binding reaction of drkN SH3 to DnaK involves a pathway whereby DnaK selects the unfolded state.
claims.source: However, the corresponding CEST traces from both residues in U show minor dips to N as well as to the bound state, unambiguously demonstrating that the major flux for the binding reaction involves a pathway whereby DnaK selects the unfolded state of drkN SH3.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is based on analysis of CEST profiles.

claims.claim: The CEST profiles of drkN SH3 bound to DnaK/ADP do not show any signature of binding/release.
claims.source: In contrast to DnaK/ATP, the CEST profiles of drkN SH3 bound to DnaK/ADP do not show any signature of binding/release (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B), though the presence of the bound states B1 and B2 can clearly be discerned from 13C-1H HMQC spectra recorded on the same sample.
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from CEST data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: The slow rates of substrate release from DnaK/ADP (~0.001 s−1, 25°C) place the exchange process outside the window of detection via CEST methods.
claims.source: This is a consequence of the slow rates of substrate release from DnaK/ADP (~0.001 s−1, 25°C) (Mayer and Bukau, 2005; Pierpaoli et al., 1998), which places the exchange process outside the window of detection via CEST methods (Vallurupalli et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This explanation is supported by citations to prior literature on DnaK/ADP kinetics and CEST methodology.

claims.claim: The flux ratio Θ1 for the formation of bound state B1 (Ile 53 at position 0) of drkN SH3 with DnaK is 4.
claims.source: Using these values, Θ1 and Θ2 for the formation of bound states B1 and B2 corresponding to Ile 53 and Ile 27 of drkN SH3 at position 0 of DnaK are found to be 4 and 21 respectively.
claims.evidence: This flux ratio was calculated from rate constants obtained from fitting CEST data.

claims.claim: The flux ratio Θ2 for the formation of bound state B2 (Ile 27 at position 0) of drkN SH3 with DnaK is 21.
claims.source: Using these values, Θ1 and Θ2 for the formation of bound states B1 and B2 corresponding to Ile 53 and Ile 27 of drkN SH3 at position 0 of DnaK are found to be 4 and 21 respectively.
claims.evidence: This flux ratio was calculated from rate constants obtained from fitting CEST data.

claims.claim: No new peaks were observed in the 13C-1H HMQC spectrum upon addition of Hsc70/ATP to drkN SH3.
claims.source: Upon addition of 500 μM U-2H, Hsc70/ATP to a solution of 170 μM IM-13CH3 drkN SH3, no new peaks were observed (Figure 8A,B), suggesting that the affinity of drkN SH3 for Hsc70/ATP is lower than that for DnaK/ATP (Figure 5).
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from NMR data shown in Figure 8A,B.

claims.claim: The affinity of drkN SH3 for Hsc70/ATP is lower than that for DnaK/ATP.
claims.source: Upon addition of 500 μM U-2H, Hsc70/ATP to a solution of 170 μM IM-13CH3 drkN SH3, no new peaks were observed (Figure 8A,B), suggesting that the affinity of drkN SH3 for Hsc70/ATP is lower than that for DnaK/ATP (Figure 5).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the absence of new peaks in the spectrum.

claims.claim: The unfolded state CEST profile of Ile 27 of drkN SH3 in the presence of Hsc70/ATP shows a minor dip at ~0.33 ppm that arises from binding to Hsc70/ATP.
claims.source: Figure 8C,D shows 1H CEST profiles derived from Ile 27 of N and U drkN SH3. Similar to our observations with DnaK, the native state CEST profile (red) shows a minor dip at the frequency of Ile 27 Hδ1 in the unfolded state, while the unfolded state profile (green) shows a pair of dips, with one at the position of the native state for Ile 27 Hδ1 and a second, initially unassigned.
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from CEST data shown in Figure 8C,D.

claims.claim: The major flux to the Hsc70-bound state of drkN SH3 proceeds through the U→UK mechanism.
claims.source: Taken together our results thus confirm that the major flux to UK proceeds through U so that human Hsc70 also employs a CS mode of interaction with the drkN SH3 client protein.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is based on analysis of CEST profiles.

claims.claim: The Hsp70 client binding site sequence and architecture have been highly conserved through evolution.
claims.source: The Hsp70 family of chaperones are integral to the quality control machinery in organisms ranging from bacteria to humans and the Hsp70 client binding site sequence and architecture have been highly conserved through evolution.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about evolutionary conservation based on established knowledge.

claims.claim: A conformational selection-based mechanism for Hsp70-substrate interactions ensures that Hsp70 will not randomly unfold properly folded and functional cellular proteins.
claims.source: A CS-based mechanism for Hsp70-substrate interactions is consistent with expectations based on Hsp70 function. First, such a binding mode ensures that Hsp70 will not randomly unfold properly folded and functional cellular proteins.
claims.evidence: This is a logical inference about the functional implications of the CS mechanism.

claims.claim: A conformational selection binding mode ensures that Hsp70 will select only misfolded intermediates lacking stable secondary and tertiary structure for refolding.
claims.source: Third, the CS binding mode ensures that Hsp70 will select only misfolded intermediates lacking stable secondary and tertiary structure for refolding rather than stably folded native conformations with exposed hydrophobic sidechains so that refolding occurs in a unidirectional manner from the misfolded to the native state.
claims.evidence: This is a logical inference about the functional implications of the CS mechanism.

claims.claim: Hsp70 binds promiscuously to its substrates, recognizing different sites containing aliphatic hydrophobic residues along the polypeptide sequence.
claims.source: The multiple Hsp70-bound conformations of R17* and drkN SH3 noted in this study reinforce our previous observations with the three-helix bundle substrate hTRF1 that Hsp70 binds promiscuously to its substrates, recognizing different sites containing aliphatic hydrophobic residues along the polypeptide sequence (Rosenzweig et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This conclusion is based on observations from the current study and supported by citation to prior work.

claims.claim: Each binding site of the substrate can be recognized by Hsp70 when it becomes exposed to the solvent in the thermally accessible unfolded state.
claims.source: Our results show that each binding site of the substrate can be recognized by Hsp70 when it becomes exposed to the solvent in the thermally accessible unfolded state, highlighting the prominent role played by conformational dynamics in this crucial protein-protein interaction.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is based on the results of the study.

claims.claim: The dominant binding process for both R17* and drkN SH3 substrates with both DnaK and human Hsc70 is via the conformational selection mechanism.
claims.source: Our results establish that the dominant binding process is via the CS mechanism for both substrates considered, and for both DnaK and human Hsc70, suggesting that the CS mode of Hsp70 recognition may be conserved.
claims.evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on NMR measurements.

claims.claim: The CS mode of Hsp70 recognition may be conserved.
claims.source: Our results establish that the dominant binding process is via the CS mechanism for both substrates considered, and for both DnaK and human Hsc70, suggesting that the CS mode of Hsp70 recognition may be conserved.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observation of CS mechanism in both bacterial and human Hsp70.

claims.claim: The structures of the Hsp70 chaperone in its ATP and ADP states are substantially different.
claims.source: The structures of the Hsp70 chaperone in its ATP (Kityk et al., 2012; Qi et al., 2013) (Figure 1D) and ADP states (Bertelsen et al., 2009) (Figure 1A) are substantially different and the conformational switch that occurs in Hsp70 upon ATP hydrolysis has been hypothesized to perform conformational work on the bound substrate and alter its structure (Mayer, 2013; Clerico et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This structural information is supported by citations and illustrated in Figures 1A and 1D.

claims.claim: The structure of the substrate in the ADP-bound, ATP-bound and nucleotide-free forms of Hsp70 are identical.
claims.source: Contrary to this hypothesis, NMR studies by our group have shown that the dominant native (i.e., unbound) and bound conformations of a substrate can be significantly different despite the fact that the structure of the substrate in the ADP-bound, ATP-bound and nucleotide-free forms of Hsp70 are identical, showing that ATP hydrolysis does not have to be coupled to a substrate conformational change in the Hsp70 chaperone system (Sekhar et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior NMR studies.

claims.claim: ATP hydrolysis does not have to be coupled to a substrate conformational change in the Hsp70 chaperone system.
claims.source: Contrary to this hypothesis, NMR studies by our group have shown that the dominant native (i.e., unbound) and bound conformations of a substrate can be significantly different despite the fact that the structure of the substrate in the ADP-bound, ATP-bound and nucleotide-free forms of Hsp70 are identical, showing that ATP hydrolysis does not have to be coupled to a substrate conformational change in the Hsp70 chaperone system (Sekhar et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This conclusion is supported by citation to prior NMR studies.

claims.claim: The binding of Hsp70 to the clathrin triskelion has been postulated to occur via local conformational fluctuations in individual clathrin molecules that transiently expose the Hsp70 binding site.
claims.source: For example, the binding of Hsp70 to the clathrin triskelion that leads to downstream uncoating of a clathrin-coated vesicle has been postulated to occur via local conformational fluctuations in individual clathrin molecules that transiently expose the Hsp70 binding site (Böcking et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claims.claim: The recognition of σ32 by E.coli Hsp70 (DnaK) has been hypothesized to occur through transient excursions of the σ32 molecule from a compact conformation to a more accessible extended structure.
claims.source: The recognition of σ32 by E.coli Hsp70 (DnaK) has also been hypothesized to occur through transient excursions of the σ32 molecule from a compact conformation where the binding site is sequestered in a helix to a more accessible extended structure (Rodriguez et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claims.claim: The IF-like unfoldase model is believed to operate in accelerating the folding of large protein substrates such as luciferase.
claims.source: In contrast, the IF-like unfoldase model is believed to operate in accelerating the folding of large protein substrates such as luciferase by transforming misfolded kinetically trapped states into unfolded but folding-competent conformations (Sharma et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claims.claim: In order to establish that a binding interaction occurs via conformational selection, it is necessary to demonstrate that a similar conformation to the bound state is sampled in the absence of the binder and to show that the formation of the complex occurs primarily via a kinetic pathway whereby the conformation resembling the bound form is selected for binding.
claims.source: In general, distinguishing between CS and IF mechanisms (Changeux and Edelstein, 2011) requires a consideration of both structure and kinetics. For example, in order to establish that a particular binding interaction occurs via CS, it is necessary both to demonstrate that a very similar conformation to that in the bound state is sampled in the absence of the binder and to show that the formation of the complex occurs primarily via a kinetic pathway whereby the conformation of the ligand that resembles the bound form is selected for binding.
claims.evidence: This is a methodological statement about how to distinguish CS from IF mechanisms.

claims.claim: Pre-sampling of a bound conformation does not automatically imply that the bound state forms from such a conformation.
claims.source: While there is compelling evidence in a number of cases for the pre-sampling of a bound conformation in the unbound state (Boehr et al., 2009; Tzeng and Kalodimos, 2009; Ye et al., 2016; Lange et al., 2008; Anthis et al., 2011; Venditti and Clore, 2012), very few reports have unequivocally established that such a conformation is on-pathway to the bound state (Birdsall et al., 1980; Daniels et al., 2014; Daniels et al., 2015; Chakrabarti et al., 2016). Indeed, pre-sampling of a bound conformation does not automatically imply that the bound state forms from such a conformation.
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: The T199A mutant of DnaK is deficient in ATP hydrolysis.
claims.source: In all experiments involving DnaK/ATP, the allosterically active T199A mutant of DnaK (McCarty and Walker, 1991) that is deficient in ATP hydrolysis was used to minimize ATP turnover during NMR data collection.
claims.evidence: This property of the T199A mutant is supported by citation.

claims.claim: The intensities of native state Met and Ile resonances of R17* decrease by a factor of 1.6 ± 0.1 upon DnaK binding.
claims.source: The intensities of native state Met and Ile resonances decrease by a factor of 1.6 ± 0.1 upon DnaK binding, consistent with solution equilibria shifting from N, and also with different 1H and 13C chemical shifts of R17* in the bound state from those in N.
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from NMR data.

claims.claim: Intensities of Ile and Met correlations derived from the unfolded state of R17* increase by 2.2 ± 0.6 fold upon DnaK binding.
claims.source: In contrast, intensities of Ile and Met correlations derived from the unfolded state increase by 2.2 ± 0.6 fold.
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from NMR data.

claims.claim: The Met and Ile residues of R17* in bound conformations have the same chemical shifts as the unfolded state.
claims.source: The simplest interpretation of the data is that the Met and Ile residues of R17* in bound conformations have the same chemical shifts as U, with the degeneracy in shifts leading to an increase, rather than a decrease in unfolded peak intensities.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed increase in unfolded peak intensities upon DnaK binding.

claims.claim: The KD of drkN SH3 for DnaK/ADP is 243 μM.
claims.source: Cavagnero and coworkers report a KD of 243 μM for drkN SH3 and DnaK/ADP (Lee et al., 2015) that is at least two orders of magnitude weaker than literature values for peptides or proteins where Leu residues can occupy position 0 (Pierpaoli et al., 1998).
claims.evidence: This KD value is cited from prior literature.

claims.claim: The KD of drkN SH3 for DnaK/ADP is at least two orders of magnitude weaker than literature values for peptides or proteins where Leu residues can occupy position 0.
claims.source: Cavagnero and coworkers report a KD of 243 μM for drkN SH3 and DnaK/ADP (Lee et al., 2015) that is at least two orders of magnitude weaker than literature values for peptides or proteins where Leu residues can occupy position 0 (Pierpaoli et al., 1998).
claims.evidence: This comparison is based on cited literature values.

claims.claim: The absence of Leu residues at the DnaK binding site may account for the low affinity of drkN SH3 for DnaK.
claims.source: The absence of Leu residues at the binding site may possibly account for the low affinity of drkN SH3 for DnaK, even in the high affinity binding state where DnaK is ADP loaded.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation based on the observation of no Leu residues at the binding site and the known preference of DnaK for Leu.

claims.claim: Peaks 1 and 2 in the drkN SH3-DnaK complex are derived from Ile 53 and Ile 27, respectively.
claims.source: This was achieved using a zz-exchange experiment that links peaks 1 and 2 to the corresponding U state correlations, that were already assigned by traditional NMR methods. In this way we could show that peaks 1 and 2 are derived from Ile 53 and Ile 27, respectively (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This assignment was made using zz-exchange data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Peaks 1 and 2 in the drkN SH3-DnaK complex report on two distinct DnaK-bound conformations labeled as B1 and B2.
claims.source: Since we know from NOE data that both peaks 1 and 2 are present at the 0 position, it follows that peaks 1 and 2 report on two distinct DnaK-bound conformations of drkN SH3, labeled as B1 and B2 respectively.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is based on NOE data and zz-exchange assignments.

claims.claim: In the B1 conformer of drkN SH3-DnaK, Ile 53 is at the 0 position.
claims.source: In the B1 conformer Ile 53 is at the 0 position while in B2 the 0 position is occupied by Ile 27.
claims.evidence: This is based on NOE data and zz-exchange assignments.

claims.claim: In the B2 conformer of drkN SH3-DnaK, Ile 27 is at the 0 position.
claims.source: In the B1 conformer Ile 53 is at the 0 position while in B2 the 0 position is occupied by Ile 27.
claims.evidence: This is based on NOE data and zz-exchange assignments.

claims.claim: 98% of the Ξ values for state B1 fall within the range of 0.84–1.27.
claims.source: In order to estimate Ξ, we fit the CEST data using a bootstrap procedure (Efron and Tibshirani, 1986) described in Materials and methods; the resulting distribution of Ξ values is narrow and centred around ~1, with 98% of the values falling within the range of 0.84–1.27 for state B1 (Ile 53 at the 0 position) and 0.49–1.57 for B2 (Ile 27 at the 0 position) (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This range was obtained from bootstrap analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: 98% of the Ξ values for state B2 fall within the range of 0.49–1.57.
claims.source: In order to estimate Ξ, we fit the CEST data using a bootstrap procedure (Efron and Tibshirani, 1986) described in Materials and methods; the resulting distribution of Ξ values is narrow and centred around ~1, with 98% of the values falling within the range of 0.84–1.27 for state B1 (Ile 53 at the 0 position) and 0.49–1.57 for B2 (Ile 27 at the 0 position) (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This range was obtained from bootstrap analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: The average and standard deviation of the Ξ distribution are 1.0 ± 0.1 for the B1 arm and 1.0 ± 0.2 for the B2 arm.
claims.source: The average and standard deviation of the Ξ distribution are 1.0 ± 0.1 and 1.0 ± 0.2 for the B1 and B2 arms respectively.
claims.evidence: These values were obtained from bootstrap analysis.

claims.claim: Θ is well approximated by the ratio kex,UB/kex,NB for drkN SH3 binding to DnaK.
claims.source: This implies that Θ is well approximated by the ratio kex,UB/kex,NB.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the narrow distribution of Ξ values around 1.

claims.claim: The chemical shift of the minor dip in the unfolded state CEST profile of drkN SH3 with Hsc70/ATP is 0.35 ppm.
claims.source: First the chemical shift of the dip, 0.35 ppm, is close to 0.2 ppm that was measured for the DnaK bound states B1 and B2 (Figure 5).
claims.evidence: This chemical shift is observed in CEST data shown in Figure 8.

claims.claim: A 13C-1H HMQC spectrum recorded after leaving the drkN SH3-Hsc70/ATP sample for approximately 2 days at room temperature shows a new peak at 0.35 ppm.
claims.source: Finally, a 13C-1H HMQC spectrum recorded after leaving the sample for approximately 2 days at room temperature, sufficient time for Hsc70/ATP to convert to Hsc70/ADP, shows a new peak at the 1H chemical shift of the minor dip, 0.35 ppm.
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from NMR data.

claims.claim: The new peak at 0.35 ppm in the drkN SH3-Hsc70 sample belongs to Hsc70/ADP-bound drkN SH3.

claims.claim: Conformational dynamics play a prominent role in the Hsp70-substrate interaction.

results.result: The manuscript describes the structural and functional properties of Hsp70 chaperones based on prior literature, including domain architecture, substrate binding mode, substrate preferences, and the globally unfolded state of bound substrates.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C10 are well-supported by multiple citations to established literature. These claims provide essential background knowledge about Hsp70 structure and function that contextualizes the current study. The structural information is illustrated in figures and consistently referenced across the field.

results.result: R17* substrate binds to DnaK/ATP, forming multiple bound conformations that are globally unfolded and structurally similar to the unfolded state U, with at least two distinct Leu residues occupying the DnaK binding site.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C15 and C55-C57 are supported by direct NMR observations (Figures 3, 3-supplements) showing new peaks upon DnaK addition, intensity changes consistent with global unfolding, and structural predictions. Claims C89-C96 provide additional structural characterization through LIMBO predictions, mutagenesis, and NOE data confirming binding sites. The convergence of multiple experimental approaches strengthens these conclusions.

results.result: For R17* binding to DnaK, zz-exchange NMR demonstrates that cross-peaks connect only the unfolded state (U) to the bound state (UK), not the native state (N) to UK, establishing conformational selection as the dominant mechanism with flux ratio Θ > 113.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C21 are strongly supported by direct experimental observations from zz-exchange NMR (Figure 4). The absence of N-UK cross-peaks (C17) combined with presence of U-UK cross-peaks (C16) provides unequivocal evidence for the CS mechanism. Quantitative flux calculations (C19-C21) are derived from fitting time-dependent data with bootstrap error analysis, providing robust kinetic parameters.

results.result: DrkN SH3 substrate binds to DnaK forming at least two distinct bound conformations (B1 with Ile 53 at position 0, B2 with Ile 27 at position 0), with the bound state structurally similar to the unfolded state and exhibiting relatively low affinity for DnaK.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C25 are supported by prior literature (C22-C23) and direct NMR observations (C24-C25, Figure 5). Claims C58-C64 provide structural characterization through NOE data, zz-exchange assignments, and affinity measurements. The convergence of spectroscopic evidence and structural assignments from multiple experiments supports these conclusions, though the speculation about Leu absence affecting affinity (C60) is appropriately qualified.

results.result: CEST NMR profiles of drkN SH3 with DnaK/ATP demonstrate that the unfolded state shows minor dips to both native and bound states, while native state profiles show dips only to unfolded state, establishing conformational selection with flux ratios Θ1=4 and Θ2=21 for the two binding sites.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C28 are supported by direct CEST observations (Figure 6). Claims C31-C32 and C65-C68 provide quantitative flux analysis from global fitting of CEST profiles with bootstrap error estimation. The four-state model fitting (Figure 7) with reduced χ² analysis demonstrates that rate constants can be reliably extracted. The narrow distribution of Ξ values around 1 justifies the approximation used for flux calculations.

results.result: CEST profiles of drkN SH3 bound to DnaK/ADP show no signatures of binding/release due to slow exchange rates (~0.001 s⁻¹) that fall outside the CEST detection window.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C30 are supported by direct CEST observations (Figure 6-supplement 1B) and citations to literature values for DnaK/ADP release rates. The explanation is consistent with the known timescale limitations of CEST methodology. This negative control strengthens the interpretation of the DnaK/ATP results.

results.result: Human Hsc70/ATP binds drkN SH3 with lower affinity than DnaK/ATP, but CEST profiles reveal a minor dip in the unfolded state at ~0.33 ppm corresponding to Hsc70-bound state, demonstrating that human Hsc70 also employs conformational selection for substrate recognition.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C37 are supported by NMR observations (Figure 8) showing no new peaks but CEST minor dips revealing the 'invisible' bound state. Claims C69-C71 provide chemical shift evidence and time-dependent conversion to ADP-bound form. Claims C73-C75 address potential NOE artifacts through control experiments with DnaK/ADP and NOESY data. The convergence of evidence supports the CS mechanism for Hsc70 despite the low-affinity interaction.

results.result: Both bacterial (DnaK) and human (Hsc70) Hsp70 chaperones interact with client proteins (R17* and drkN SH3) by selecting the unfolded state from pre-existing conformational ensembles, suggesting a conserved conformational selection mechanism across the Hsp70 family.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C43-C44 represent the main conclusions of the study, directly supported by the experimental results for both substrates and both chaperones (Claims grouped in results above). The observation of CS mechanism in both bacterial and human orthologs with structurally distinct substrates (α-helical and β-sheet) provides strong evidence for conservation. However, the generalization is appropriately qualified as 'suggesting' rather than definitively proving conservation across all Hsp70s.

results.result: The conformational selection mechanism is functionally consistent with Hsp70 biology: it prevents random unfolding of properly folded proteins, accommodates naturally unfolded substrates, ensures unidirectional refolding, and is compatible with binding sites in solvent-exposed regions.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C40 and C78-C80 provide logical inferences about functional implications supported by citations to prior literature. The evolutionary conservation of binding site architecture (C38) and the properties of known Hsp70 substrates (C79-C80) are well-documented. The functional logic connecting CS mechanism to biological outcomes is sound, though these remain inferences rather than direct experimental tests.

results.result: Hsp70 binds promiscuously to multiple sites on substrates containing aliphatic hydrophobic residues, with each site recognized when exposed in the thermally accessible unfolded state, highlighting the role of conformational dynamics in substrate recognition.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C42 and C85-C86 are supported by observations of multiple bound conformations for both R17* and drkN SH3 (C14, C62) and reinforced by prior work on hTRF1. The conclusion about conformational dynamics is a direct inference from the CS mechanism established experimentally. The promiscuous binding is demonstrated by NOE data showing different residues at position 0.

results.result: The structures of Hsp70 in ATP and ADP states differ substantially, but substrate structure remains identical across nucleotide states, demonstrating that ATP hydrolysis need not be coupled to substrate conformational changes.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C47 are supported by citations to structural studies (C45) and prior NMR work from the authors' group (C46-C47). This provides important context for interpreting the current results, showing that the CS mechanism is consistent with prior findings that substrate conformation is independent of chaperone nucleotide state.

results.result: Prior literature has proposed both CS-like mechanisms (for clathrin and σ32 binding) and IF-like unfoldase mechanisms (for luciferase folding) for different Hsp70-substrate systems.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C50 accurately summarize prior hypotheses from cited literature. These provide important context for the current study's mechanistic investigation. The claims are appropriately qualified as 'postulated' or 'hypothesized' and are well-supported by citations.

results.result: Distinguishing CS from IF mechanisms requires demonstrating both structural similarity between unbound and bound states AND showing that complex formation proceeds via the kinetic pathway selecting the bound-like conformation; pre-sampling alone is insufficient evidence.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C52 provide methodological framework supported by citations to prior literature. This establishes the rigorous criteria applied in the current study and justifies the experimental approach combining structural (NMR chemical shifts) and kinetic (exchange rates, flux analysis) measurements. The distinction is critical for proper interpretation of results.

results.result: The CS mechanism conclusions pertain to elementary binding steps involving large conformational differences (N vs U); small structural differences between UK and U states may exist but cannot be definitively assigned to CS or IF pathways, and broader multistep unfoldase mechanisms are not excluded.
results.evaluation: Claims C77 and C81-C84 provide appropriate caveats and scope limitations for the study's conclusions. These are logical inferences based on the experimental design and detection limits. The acknowledgment that Hsp70 divides substrates into segments (C82) and disrupts tertiary interactions (C83, supported by prior citation) demonstrates careful consideration of mechanistic complexity.

results.result: The T199A DnaK mutant deficient in ATP hydrolysis was used to study the ATP state, which represents an important entry point to the chaperone cycle with millisecond-timescale substrate complex lifetimes suitable for CEST methodology.
results.evaluation: Claims C54, C87-C88 describe methodological choices supported by citations to prior literature. The use of the T199A mutant is well-justified for maintaining ATP-bound state during NMR data collection. The timescale considerations are appropriate for the experimental methods employed.

results.result: Hsc70/ADP has higher affinity for substrate than Hsc70/ATP.
results.evaluation: Claim C72 represents established knowledge about Hsp70 chaperones, used to interpret the appearance of a new peak after ATP-to-ADP conversion (C70-C71). This is well-documented in the literature and consistent with the known allosteric regulation of Hsp70.

results.result: Prior structural and biophysical studies establish that Ile 401 and Ile 438 are within 5 Å of substrate residue at position 0, NOEs can link these residues to identify binding conformations, and DnaK-bound substrates are globally unfolded.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C93 and C97 summarize well-established structural knowledge from prior literature, providing the basis for NOE-based assignment strategies used in the current study. These are appropriately cited and form the foundation for interpreting the experimental data.
